claims.claim: The Cardiff Giant was a ten-foot stone figure that was never a living being
claims.quote: It was a 10-foot-tall (3.0 m), roughly 3,000 pound purported "petrified man"

claims.claim: Well-diggers found the giant behind a barn in Cardiff, New York, on 16 October 1869
claims.quote: uncovered on October 16, 1869, by workers digging a well behind the barn of William C. "Stub" Newell, in Cardiff, New York

claims.claim: The giant weighed 2,990 pounds
claims.quote: it weighed 2,990 pounds (1,360 kg)

claims.claim: The photograph of the giant is a Bain News Service image dated 1910
claims.quote: Date: 1910 Author: Bain News Service, publisher

claims.claim: A print advertised the giant's measurements to the inch
claims.quote: ITS DIMENSIONS ARE

claims.claim: Length 10 feet 4½ inches
claims.quote: Whole length of the figure, 10 feet, 4½ inches

claims.claim: Nose 6 inches
claims.quote: length of nose, 6 inches

claims.claim: Mouth 4 inches
claims.quote: width of mouth, 4 inches

claims.claim: Foot 1 foot 7½ inches
claims.quote: length of foot, 1 foot 7½ inches

claims.claim: Shoulder to shoulder, 3 feet
claims.quote: point to point of shoulder, 3 feet

claims.claim: The print is titled "The Onondaga Giant" and credited to Popular Graphic Arts
claims.quote: THE ONONDAGA GIANT.

claims.claim: The quarrymen were told they were cutting a monument to Abraham Lincoln
claims.quote: hired men to quarry out a 10-foot-4.5-inch-long (3.2 m) block of gypsum in Fort Dodge, Iowa, telling them it was intended for a monument to Abraham Lincoln in New York

claims.claim: In 1868 the block was cut from the gypsum quarry pictured at Fort Dodge, Iowa
claims.quote: This is the Gypsum Quarry from which was taken the block out of which the original "Cardiff Giant" was carved.

claims.claim: The block was shipped to Chicago to be carved
claims.quote: The block was taken to Chicago, the "Giant" carved, and then shipped to the point in New York which gave it its name

claims.claim: The quarry stereograph is a view of Cardiff Glen, Iowa, dated 1873
claims.quote: VIEW IN CARDIFF GLEN. NEAR FORT DODGE, IOWA.

claims.claim: A tobacconist buried the giant in order to win a Bible argument
claims.quote: Hull, a skeptic, being the minority party, lost the argument. Angered by his defeat and the credulity of people, Hull wanted to prove how easily he could fool people with a fake giant.

claims.claim: George Hull confessed on 10 December 1869
claims.quote: On December 10, 1869, Hull confessed everything to the press

claims.claim: It is still unclear whether the Chicago stonecutter knew what he was carving
claims.quote: While it is not clear if Burkhardt was aware of Hull's intentions

claims.claim: The stereocard reverse is dated 1873 and held by the New York Public Library
claims.quote: Date: 1873 Author: Scan by NYPL

claims.claim: The Cardiff Giant was not genuine
claims.quote: The Cardiff Giant was one of the most famous archaeological hoaxes in American history.

claims.claim: It was carved from a block of gypsum in a Chicago workshop
claims.quote: He shipped the block to Edward Burkhardt in Chicago, a German stonecutter. Burkhardt hired two sculptors named Henry Salle and Fred Mohrmann to create the giant.

claims.claim: It was buried in a farm field and dug up a year later on cue
claims.quote: On a night in late November 1868, the giant was buried in a hole in Newell's farm. Nearly a year later, Newell hired Gideon Emmons and Henry Nichols, ostensibly to dig a well, and on October 16, 1869, they found the giant.

claims.claim: George Hull was a New York tobacconist and a skeptic who lost an argument at a Methodist revival meeting about the Genesis verse saying giants once lived on Earth
claims.quote: Hull got into an argument with Reverend Turk and his supporters at a Methodist revival meeting about Genesis 6:4, which states that there were giants who once lived on Earth. Hull, a skeptic, being the minority party, lost the argument.

claims.claim: Hull decided to prove how easily people could be fooled
claims.quote: Hull wanted to prove how easily he could fool people with a fake giant

claims.claim: In 1868 he had a 10-foot-4½-inch block quarried at Fort Dodge, Iowa
claims.quote: In 1868, Hull, accompanied by a man named H. B. Martin, hired men to quarry out a 10-foot-4.5-inch-long (3.2 m) block of gypsum in Fort Dodge, Iowa

claims.claim: Sculptors in Chicago hung quilts to muffle the sound of carving
claims.quote: it is reported that they took steps to cover up their work during the carving, putting up quilts to lessen the sound of carving

claims.claim: The figure was shaped to imitate Hull's own body
claims.quote: The giant was designed to imitate the form of Hull himself.

claims.claim: Hull consulted a geologist, learned hair would not petrify, and left the giant hairless
claims.quote: Hull consulted a geologist and learned that hairs would not be petrified, so he removed the hair and beard from the giant.

claims.claim: The skin was beaten with steel knitting needles set in a board to fake pores, then washed with sulphuric acid to age the stone
claims.quote: The giant's surface was beaten with steel knitting needles embedded in a board to simulate pores. The giant was also rubbed with sulphuric acid to create a deeper, vintage-like color.

claims.claim: It was buried behind his cousin William Newell's barn in November 1868
claims.quote: During November 1868, Hull transported the giant by railroad to the farm of his cousin, William Newell.

claims.claim: On 16 October 1869 hired well-diggers found it
claims.quote: Newell hired Gideon Emmons and Henry Nichols, ostensibly to dig a well, and on October 16, 1869, they found the giant

claims.claim: Newell charged fifty cents for a fifteen-minute viewing
claims.quote: Newell charged each visitor fifty cents for a fifteen-minute session of viewing the giant

claims.claim: Three to five hundred people came per day
claims.quote: The number of visitors went to about three to five hundred per day

claims.claim: Yale paleontologist Othniel C. Marsh called it "a most decided humbug", citing fresh tool marks on soluble gypsum
claims.quote: Yale paleontologist Othniel C. Marsh examined the statue, pointing out that it was made of soluble gypsum, which, had it been buried in its blanket of wet earth for centuries, would not still have fresh tool marks on it (which it did), and termed it "a most decided humbug"

claims.claim: Cornell's first president noted there was no sensible reason to dig a well in that spot
claims.quote: Andrew D. White, the first president of Cornell University, made a close inspection of the Cardiff Giant. He noticed that there was no good reason to try to dig a well in the exact spot the giant had been found.

claims.claim: Hull sold his interest for $23,000
claims.quote: Hull sold his part-interest for $23,000 (equivalent to $586,000 in 2025) to a syndicate of five men headed by David Hannum

claims.claim: P. T. Barnum's $50,000 offer was refused, and he had a copy modelled in wax and then exhibited it as the real giant
claims.quote: showman P. T. Barnum offered $50,000 for the giant. When the syndicate refused, he hired a man to model the giant's shape covertly in wax and create a plaster copy. He displayed his giant in New York, claiming that his was the real giant

claims.claim: Syndicate head David Hannum said "There's a sucker born every minute" of people paying to see Barnum's copy
claims.quote: David Hannum was quoted as saying, "There's a sucker born every minute" in reference to spectators paying to see Barnum's giant

claims.claim: The line is usually misattributed to Barnum
claims.quote: Since then, the quotation has often been misattributed to Barnum himself.

claims.claim: Both giants were declared fakes in court on 2 February 1870
claims.quote: on February 2, 1870, both giants were revealed as fakes in court

claims.claim: The Popular Graphic Arts print dates from 1869
claims.quote: Entered according to Act of Congress, in the year 1869, by A.L. Edwards

claims.claim: Both sides of an 1873 stereocard of Cardiff Glen, Iowa, come from the New York Public Library
claims.quote: View in Cardiff Glen, near Fort Dodge, Iowa (NYPL b11707469-G90F191 001B).tiff
